title: Kshamavani, the Jain day
hook: at the end of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of all beings: micchami dukkadam

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yom Kippur. Your line was atonement. Did you find your hour? This week took us from family feuds to your younger self, to reconciling, to a new telling, to bedtime, to the Day of Atonement. Today it closes with two words sent in every direction. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

The same two words arrive from all over in one morning. A coworker's message. A cousin's post. A card from a neighbor. Micchami dukkadam. No context, no list of what went wrong, just the phrase, sent to people near and far. For Jains, it's the day at the end of Paryushana, a season of fasting, study and self-examination. Jains call the closing day by more than one name; one of them is Kshamavani, the day of forgiveness. And the forgiveness asked for on that day doesn't stop at friends and family. It reaches every living thing.
screen: `TWO WORDS, MANY DIRECTIONS.` → `THE END OF PARYUSHANA.` → `EVERY LIVING THING.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Micchami dukkadam comes from Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures. Jains explain it as asking that whatever wrong I did be in vain, undone, without fruit. It's a request, not a speech. Nobody has to name what happened. Second, the verse behind it. Jains recite a short verse in their rite of repentance, called pratikramana. In paraphrase: I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all, and enmity with none. Notice it goes both ways in one breath: I forgive, and forgive me. Third, how wide it reaches. In Jain teaching, all living beings means exactly that: not only people, but animals, insects, the smallest creatures, the ones harmed without anyone noticing. That fits ahimsa, the Jain teaching of doing no harm. So when someone asks forgiveness on this day, they're asking it of a whole world they've moved through all year, often carelessly. Fourth, why ask strangers too. The message goes out to people you may not have wronged at all, or don't remember wronging. That's the point. It doesn't wait for a complaint. It assumes that in a year of living, a person has stepped on more toes than they know about, and it clears the ground anyway. Two words, sent wide, asking to start the next season clean.
screen: `LET MY WRONG BE IN VAIN.` · `I FORGIVE, AND FORGIVE ME.` · `ALL LIVING BEINGS.` · `IT DOESN'T WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT.` · then, large: `MICCHAMI DUKKADAM.`

segments.voice: Sit, and let the breath slow. Start close: one person you know you've hurt this year. Hold them in mind for a few breaths. Then widen. People you may have hurt without knowing: a short reply, a missed call, someone you talked over. Then wider: the creatures you stepped past, the ones whose homes your life touches. You don't need a list. Just let the circle grow, breath by breath, until it's bigger than you can see. If it fits for you, silently offer the Jain phrase, micchami dukkadam, to the whole circle. If you pray, you can do this in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Kshamavani. The Jain day of forgiveness at the close of Paryushana, when people ask pardon of all living beings. Today's word.
Your line: micchami dukkadam. Today, send a short message to one person you've hurt, in your own words, asking their forgiveness. No explanation needed. Day nine hundred ninety-four.

howItsDone: At the close of Paryushana, Jains ask forgiveness of family, friends, neighbors and all living beings, in person, by letter or by message, with the words micchami dukkadam; the pratikramana rite includes a verse forgiving and asking forgiveness of all beings.

original.note: Prakrit, the language of the Jain scriptures, written here in Devanagari.

trapdoor: what you thought: micchami dukkadam is a Jain way of saying sorry.
what it means: a request that whatever wrong I did be in vain, sent to all living beings.
what a scholar hears: the phrase belongs to pratikramana, the Jain rite of turning back from faults, and the day widens it to the whole world.

notes: No public-domain English translation of the khamemi verse is quoted; the paraphrase ('I forgive all living beings; may all living beings forgive me; friendship with all, enmity with none') should be checked against the Prakrit (khāmemi savva jīve, savve jīvā khamantu me, mittī me savva bhūesu, veraṃ majjha na keṇai).

Names of the day differ: Svetambara Jains commonly speak of Samvatsari at the end of Paryushana, Digambara Jains of Kshamavani after Das Lakshana. The voice says only that 'Jains call the closing day by more than one name'; a Keeper should confirm the wording and whether to mention both.
The meaning of micchami dukkadam is attributed to Jain explanation ('may my wrong be fruitless / in vain'); confirm the gloss and the Devanagari spelling.
'Prakrit, the old language of the Jain scriptures' (Ardhamagadhi Prakrit for the Svetambara canon): confirm.
Editor pass: review no longer says the Jain day 'reaches further than any of' the others, which ranked it above Yom Kippur.

Audit pass: no textual errors found. khāmemi is translated both 'I forgive' and 'I ask pardon of' by modern scholars; the paraphrase keeps the two-way sense. Keep the Samvatsari/Kshamavani naming note open for a Keeper.
